subtype: Approach: time-boxed daily schedule with fixed slots [Action]
passage: Santosh, let me, Harsha, tell you how I got through my exam year. Before I started, I drew the day on a sheet: 6 to 9 study, tea, 10 to 1 second block, lunch, a nap, 3 to 6 third block, then a walk, then dinner, and lights out at 10:30. Sunday evening was for one review of the week. Simple. The trouble came in week three. One morning I woke up with no wish to open a book. I thought, what is the point? My mother did not say a word. She left tea on the desk at six. I looked at the sheet and sat down. Not because I felt like it, but because the sheet said so. Half an hour later the wish came back.

qa.q: What time was lights out on Harsha's schedule?
What was Harsha feeling on the morning of week three?
qa.a: Harsha felt flat and unmotivated, wondering what the point was and having no wish to open a book.

qa.q: What choice inside the story turned that morning around, and why?
qa.a: Harsha sat down because the sheet said so, not because Harsha felt like it, and starting anyway brought the wish back after half an hour.

qa.q: How might Harsha's mother have seen that morning?
qa.a: Harsha's mother said nothing and left tea on the desk at six, so she seems to have trusted the routine and offered quiet support instead of pressure.

grounding: Shows a fixed daily timetable with study blocks, breaks, sleep and a weekly review that is followed on days when the wish to study is missing.

subtype: Approach: time-boxed daily schedule with fixed slots [Action]
passage: Zubin's timetable for the civil services prelims was taped above his desk in their small Nagpur flat: 7 to 9:30 study, 30-minute break, 10 to 12:30, lunch, 2 to 4:30, walk, 6 to 8, dinner, lights out at 10:30. Sunday evening: one hour to review the week. Then his cousin Ganga's wedding arrived, and the flat filled with relatives, a dholak in the living room, and his mother needing help with everything. Zubin's motivation, already low in the fourth month, sank further. He didn't abandon the timetable. He moved it. The 7 am block went up to the terrace, before anyone woke. The afternoon block shrank to ninety minutes in the building's quiet stairwell. He still slept at 10:30, even on the night of the sangeet, leaving early with a plate of food. On Sunday, reviewing his log, he had kept seventy percent of his hours. Not perfect. Enough.

qa.q: What time is lights out on Zubin's timetable?
How was Zubin feeling during the wedding week?
qa.a: Zubin felt low and unmotivated, already in the fourth month and with the flat full of noise and relatives.

qa.q: What else could Zubin do next time a family event comes?
qa.a: Zubin could plan a lighter version of the timetable for that week in advance, so the change is a choice, not a scramble.

qa.q: How might Ganga see Zubin leaving the sangeet early?
qa.a: Ganga might feel a little sad he left early, but may understand, since he joined in, ate with the family and kept his exam goals.

grounding: Shows an aspirant keeping a daily timetable of study blocks, breaks, fixed sleep and a weekly review, and following it even when motivation dips.

subtype: Approach: time-boxed daily schedule with fixed slots [Action]
passage: In her paying-guest room in Delhi's Mukherjee Nagar, Aparna's day was a grid on the wall: four study blocks of two and a half hours, a thirty-minute break after each, lights out at 11, and a one-hour review every Saturday at 5. Her roommate Aadhya, preparing for the same exam, studied in bursts, sometimes ten hours, sometimes none. In the second month, a grey week came. Aparna woke up heavy, scrolled her phone in bed, and felt no reason to open the polity book. She looked at the grid. "You don't have to feel like it," she told herself. "You just have to sit down at 7." She did. The first hour was slow; by the second she was taking notes. That Saturday, her review showed twenty-six blocks out of twenty-eight done. Aadhya, flat on her bed after another zero day, asked quietly, "Can you make me a grid too?"

qa.a: Every Saturday at 5, for one hour.

qa.q: How was Aparna feeling during the grey week?
qa.a: Aparna felt heavy and unmotivated, scrolling in bed with no wish to open the polity book.

qa.q: What else could help Aparna on low days?
qa.a: Aparna could make the first block of a low day an easier task, like revision, so starting feels lighter while the routine stays.

qa.q: How is Aadhya affected by Aparna's routine?
qa.a: Aadhya, worn out by burst-and-crash days, sees the steady routine working and asks for a grid too.

grounding: Illustrates an aspirant with fixed study blocks, breaks, sleep time and a weekly review who keeps to the grid through a low-motivation week.
